fetched_contents.text: Greenhouse effect Atmospheric heat retention This article is about atmospheric heat retention. For the general heating or cooling of Earth's surface, see Earth's energy budget. For other uses, see Greenhouse (disambiguation). The greenhouse effect occurs when heat-trapping gases in a planet's atmosphere prevent the planet from losing heat to space, raising its surface temperature. Surface heating can happen from an internal heat source (as in the case of Jupiter) or come from an external source, such as a host star. In the case of Earth, the Sun emits shortwave radiation (sunlight) that passes through greenhouse gases to heat the Earth's surface. In response, the Earth's surface emits longwave radiation that is mostly absorbed by greenhouse gases, reducing the rate at which the Earth can cool off. Without the greenhouse effect, the Earth's average surface temperature would be as cold as −18 °C (−0.4 °F).[1][2] This is much less than the 20th century average of about 14 °C (57 °F).[3][4] In addition to naturally present greenhouse gases, burning of fossil fuels has increased amounts of carbon dioxide and methane in the atmosphere.[5][6] As a result, at 2023,[7] global warming of about 1.2 °C (2.2 °F) has occurred since the Industrial Revolution,[8] with the global average surface temperature increasing at a rate of 0.18 °C (0.32 °F) per decade since 1981.[9] All objects with a temperature above absolute zero emit thermal radiation. The wavelengths of thermal radiation emitted by the Sun and Earth differ because their surface temperatures are different. The Sun has a surface temperature of 5,500 °C (9,900 °F), so it emits most of its energy as shortwave radiation in near-infrared and visible wavelengths (as sunlight). In contrast, Earth's surface has a much lower temperature, so it emits longwave radiation at mid- and far-infrared wavelengths.[6] A gas is a greenhouse gas if it absorbs longwave radiation. Earth's atmosphere absorbs only 23% of incoming shortwave radiation, but absorbs 90% of the longwave radiation emitted by the surface,[10] thus accumulating energy and warming the Earth's surface. The existence of the greenhouse effect (while not named as such) was proposed as early as 1824 by Joseph Fourier.[11] The argument and the evidence were further strengthened by Claude Pouillet in 1827 and 1838. In 1856 Eunice Newton Foote demonstrated that the warming effect of the sun is greater for air with water vapour than for dry air, and the effect is even greater with carbon dioxide.[12][13] The term greenhouse was first applied to this phenomenon by Nils Gustaf Ekholm in 1901.[14][15] Definition The greenhouse effect on Earth is defined as: "The infrared radiative effect of all infrared absorbing constituents in the atmosphere. Greenhouse gases (GHGs), clouds, and some aerosols absorb terrestrial radiation emitted by the Earth's surface and elsewhere in the atmosphere."[16]: 2232 The enhanced greenhouse effect describes the fact that by increasing the concentration of GHGs in the atmosphere (due to human action), the natural greenhouse effect is increased.[16]: 2232 Terminology The term greenhouse effect comes from an analogy to greenhouses. Both greenhouses and the greenhouse effect work by retaining heat from sunlight, but the way they retain heat differs. Greenhouses retain heat mainly by blocking convection (the movement of air).[17][18] In contrast, the greenhouse effect retains heat by restricting radiative transfer through the air and reducing the rate at which thermal radiation is emitted into space.[5] History of discovery and investigation See also: History of climate change science Eunice Newton Foote recognized carbon dioxide's heat-capturing effect in 1856, appreciating its implications for the planet.[19] The greenhouse effect and its impact on climate were succinctly described in this 1912 Popular Mechanics article, accessible for reading by the general public. The existence of the greenhouse effect, while not named as such, was proposed as early as 1824 by Joseph Fourier.[11] The argument and the evidence were further strengthened by Claude Pouillet in 1827 and 1838. In 1856 Eunice Newton Foote demonstrated that the warming effect of the sun is greater for air with water vapour than for dry air, and the effect is even greater with carbon dioxide. She concluded that "An atmosphere of that gas would give to our earth a high temperature..."[12][13] John Tyndall was the first to measure the infrared absorption and emission of various gases and vapors. From 1859 onwards, he showed that the effect was due to a very small proportion of the atmosphere, with the main gases having no effect, and was largely due to water vapor, though small percentages of hydrocarbons and carbon dioxide had a significant effect.[20] The effect was more fully quantified by Svante Arrhenius in 1896, who made the first quantitative prediction of global warming due to a hypothetical doubling of atmospheric carbon dioxide.[21] The term greenhouse was first applied to this phenomenon by Nils Gustaf Ekholm in 1901.[14][15] This section is an excerpt from History of climate change science § First calculations of greenhouse effect, 1896. In 1896 Svante Arrhenius used Langley's observations of increased infrared absorption where Moon rays pass through the atmosphere at a low angle, encountering more carbon dioxide (CO2), to estimate an atmospheric cooling effect from a future decrease of CO2. He realized that the cooler atmosphere would hold less water vapor (another greenhouse gas) and calculated the additional cooling effect. He also realized the cooling would increase snow and ice cover at high latitudes, making the planet reflect more sunlight and thus further cool down, as James Croll had hypothesized. Overall Arrhenius calculated that cutting CO2 in half would suffice to produce an ice age. fetched_contents.text: Outgoing longwave radiation Energy transfer mechanism which enables planetary cooling In climate science, longwave radiation (LWR) is electromagnetic thermal radiation emitted by Earth's surface, atmosphere, and clouds. It is also referred to as terrestrial radiation. This radiation is in the infrared portion of the spectrum, but is distinct from the shortwave (SW) near-infrared radiation found in sunlight.[1]: 2251 Outgoing longwave radiation (OLR) is the longwave radiation emitted to space from the top of Earth's atmosphere.[1]: 2241 It may also be referred to as emitted terrestrial radiation. Outgoing longwave radiation plays an important role in planetary cooling. Longwave radiation generally spans wavelengths ranging from 3–100 micrometres (μm). A cutoff of 4 μm is sometimes used to differentiate sunlight from longwave radiation. Less than 1% of sunlight has wavelengths greater than 4 μm. Over 99% of outgoing longwave radiation has wavelengths between 4 μm and 100 μm.[2] The flux of energy transported by outgoing longwave radiation is typically measured in units of watts per metre squared (W⋅m−2). In the case of global energy flux, the W/m2 value is obtained by dividing the total energy flow over the surface of the globe (measured in watts) by the surface area of the Earth, 5.1×1014 m2 (5.1×108 km2; 2.0×108 mi2).[3] Emitting outgoing longwave radiation is the only way Earth loses energy to space, i.e., the only way the planet cools itself.[4] Radiative heating from absorbed sunlight, and radiative cooling to space via OLR power the heat engine that drives atmospheric dynamics.[5] The balance between OLR (energy lost) and incoming solar shortwave radiation (energy gained) determines whether the Earth is experiencing global heating or cooling (see Earth's energy budget).[6] Planetary energy balance Outgoing longwave radiation (OLR) constitutes a critical component of Earth's energy budget.[9] The principle of conservation of energy says that energy cannot appear or disappear. Thus, any energy that enters a system but does not leave must be retained within the system. So, the amount of energy retained on Earth (in Earth's climate system) is governed by an equation: [change in Earth's energy] = − . Energy arrives in the form of absorbed solar radiation (ASR). Energy leaves as outgoing longwave radiation (OLR). Thus, the rate of change in the energy in Earth's climate system is given by Earth's energy imbalance (EEI): E E I = A S R − O L R {\displaystyle \mathrm {EEI} =\mathrm {ASR} -\mathrm {OLR} } . When energy is arriving at a higher rate than it leaves (i.e., ASR > OLR, so that EEI is positive), the amount of energy in Earth's climate increases. Temperature is a measure of the amount of thermal energy in matter. So, under these circumstances, temperatures tend to increase overall (though temperatures might decrease in some places as the distribution of energy changes). As temperatures increase, the amount of thermal radiation emitted also increases, leading to more outgoing longwave radiation (OLR), and a smaller energy imbalance (EEI).[10] Similarly, if energy arrives at a lower rate than it leaves (i.e., ASR < OLR, so than EEI is negative), the amount of energy in Earth's climate decreases, and temperatures tend to decrease overall. As temperatures decrease, OLR decreases, making the imbalance closer to zero.[10] In this fashion, a planet naturally constantly adjusts its temperature so as to keep the energy imbalance small. If there is more solar radiation absorbed than OLR emitted, the planet will heat up. If there is more OLR than absorbed solar radiation the planet will cool. In both cases, the temperature change works to shift the energy imbalance towards zero. When the energy imbalance is zero, a planet is said to be in radiative equilibrium. Planets naturally tend to a state of approximate radiative equilibrium.[10] In recent decades, energy has been measured to be arriving on Earth at a higher rate than it leaves, corresponding to planetary warming. The energy imbalance has been increasing.[7][8] It can take decades to centuries for oceans to warm and planetary temperature to shift sufficiently to compensate for an energy imbalance.[11] Emission Thermal radiation is emitted by nearly all matter, in proportion to the fourth power of its absolute temperature. In particular, the emitted energy flux, M {\displaystyle M} (measured in W/m2) is given by the Stefan–Boltzmann law for non-blackbody matter:[12] M = ϵ σ T 4 {\displaystyle M=\epsilon \,\sigma \,T^{4}} where T {\displaystyle T} is the absolute temperature, σ {\displaystyle \sigma } is the Stefan–Boltzmann constant, and ϵ {\displaystyle \epsilon } is the emissivity. The emissivity is a value between zero and one which indicates how much less radiation is emitted compared to what a perfect blackbody would emit. Surface The emissivity of Earth's surface has been measured to be in the range 0.65 to 0.99 (based on observations in the 8-13 micron wavelength range) with the lowest values being for barren desert regions. The emissivity is mostly above 0.9, and the global average surface emissivity is estimated to be around 0.95.[13][14] Atmosphere The most common gases in air (i.e., nitrogen, oxygen, and argon) have a negligible ability to absorb or emit longwave thermal radiation. Consequently, the ability of air to absorb and emit longwave radiation is determined by the concentration of trace gases like water vapor and carbon dioxide.[15] According to Kirchhoff's law of thermal radiation, the emissivity of matter is always equal to its absorptivity, at a given wavelength.[12] At some wavelengths, greenhouse gases absorb 100% of the longwave radiation emitted by the surface.[16] So, at those wavelengths, the emissivity of the atmosphere is 1 and the atmosphere emits thermal radiation much like an ideal blackbody would. fetched_contents.text: WXWISE ERBE The Earth's Radiation Energy Balance An object will warm or cool depending on its energy imbalances. If the object receives more energy than it losses, the object will warm. If the object losses more energy than it receives it will cool, and if the energy gains equal the energy losses, there is no temperature change. Methods of transferring energy in the atmosphere include conduction, convection, latent heating, advection and radiation. The method of transferring energy through radiative processes is different from the other mechanisms in that the transfer process does not require molecules. If we consider the planet as a whole, the Earth exchanges energy with its environment (the solar system) via radiation. The radiation balance of the planet is a fundamental parameter that determines our climate. This balance includes energy from the sun, or solar energy, which is an energy source for the planet. Any object that has a temperature emits radiation, we refer to this energy as terrestrial or infrared energy. The hotter the object, the greater the amount of energy emitted. Terrestrial energy can cool or warm an object depending on the object's temperature, and the temperature of the surrounding environment. Imagine that you are at a barn fire on a cool autumn evening. As you face the fire, your front warms because you are receiving more energy from the fire than you are losing. Your back cools down and gets cold because you are losing more energy than you receive from the cooler air around you. You experience a local energy imbalance, your front warms and your back gets cold. If you get too uncomfortable, you can turn around, allowing your back to warm-up and your front to cool-down. As we look at the radiation balance of the planet, just because a given region may be receiving more radiative energy than it is losing does not mean the region's temperature is increasing. Clouds reduce outgoing longwave radiation (OLR) by both blocking surface radiation and emitting longwave radiation in multiple directions. Directly, clouds absorb some of the longwave radiation emitted by the surface and re-emit it, with some rays going downward toward the surface and some upward toward space. The NASA Science source describes longwave rays emitted by Earth being absorbed and reemitted by a cloud, with some rays going to the surface, indicating that clouds act as a partial barrier to surface emission while also redistributing energy [N2-R3]. The same source also says clouds reduce the radiation emission to space and thus result in a heating of the planet, which means clouds do not simply allow OLR to escape unchanged [N3-F3].

Clouds also block outgoing longwave radiation from the surface by absorbing part of that radiation before it can escape to space. The NASA source explicitly states that clouds interact with and absorb some radiation, causing the atmosphere to warm, and the OLR reduction is a key part of this effect [N3-R1]. In the broader Earth energy budget context, clouds reduce the radiation emission to space, so the surface emits less of its longwave radiation directly to space, and more of it is intercepted and reemitted by the clouds [N3-F3]. This is why clouds are described as reducing Earth’s OLR on average by about 30 W·m⁻² [N2-R5].

Cloud optical thickness and altitude change the effect because thicker clouds are more opaque and absorb more radiation, while higher clouds are colder and emit less longwave radiation. The evidence shows that larger aerosol particles and clouds can interact with and absorb radiation, and that cloud coverage strongly affects the planetary albedo and OLR [N3-R1]. In the Earth radiation budget context, the strength of the cloud effect depends on cloud properties, and the ERBE discussion notes that cloud-free ocean regions have low albedos, while persistent low-level clouds are associated with high albedos, showing how cloud characteristics alter radiative exchange [N3-F3]. Although the provided evidence does not give a numerical altitude-dependent formula, it does support the general principle that cloud altitude and thickness determine how much radiation is absorbed versus re-emitted [N2-R3][N3-F3].

Overall, clouds reduce OLR by absorbing part of the surface’s longwave emission, re-emitting it downward and upward, and thereby reducing the amount of longwave radiation that escapes directly to space [N2-R3][N3-F3]. This makes clouds a key radiative component in Earth’s climate system, contributing both warming and cooling depending on context [N3-R3].

## How the atmosphere and clouds reduce Earth's outgoing longwave radiation

The atmosphere and clouds reduce Earth's outgoing longwave radiation (OLR) by absorbing and re-emitting longwave radiation, which means less energy escapes directly to space. This process is central to the greenhouse effect and Earth’s climate system.

### 1) Atmospheric absorption and emission of longwave radiation

The atmosphere does not absorb or emit longwave radiation mainly because of nitrogen, oxygen, and argon; those gases have negligible ability to do so [N2-F2]. Instead, the ability of air to absorb and emit longwave radiation is determined by trace greenhouse gases like water vapor and carbon dioxide [N2-F2]. Greenhouse gases absorb most of the longwave radiation emitted by the Earth [N1-R3], and the Earth’s atmosphere absorbs about 90% of the longwave radiation emitted by the surface [N1-F1]. This means that much of the energy radiated upward from the surface is intercepted before it can escape to space.

The atmosphere then re-emits that radiation in all directions, including back toward the surface and out to space [N1-F1][N2-F2]. This is a key mechanism: instead of allowing longwave radiation to escape directly, the atmosphere redistributes it. The greenhouse-effect source explains that the infrared radiative effect of all infrared-absorbing constituents in the atmosphere is the greenhouse effect, and that it restricts radiative transfer through the air and reduces the rate at which thermal radiation is emitted into space [N1-F1]. So, the atmosphere does not simply transmit longwave radiation; it absorbs it and then emits it again, reducing the amount of energy that escapes unimpeded.

Absorption reduces the amount of energy escaping to space because the atmosphere intercepts outgoing longwave radiation before it reaches space [N1-R1]. The Wikipedia source on outgoing longwave radiation also says that outgoing longwave radiation is the longwave radiation emitted to space from the top of Earth’s atmosphere, and that energy is the only way the planet cools itself [N2-F2]. Therefore, when greenhouse gases absorb outgoing longwave radiation, they reduce the net amount that escapes to space [N1-R1][N2-F2].

### 2) Clouds reduce outgoing longwave radiation by blocking and re-emitting radiation

Clouds also reduce outgoing longwave radiation by absorbing some of the longwave radiation emitted by the surface and re-emitting it in multiple directions. The evidence says that longwave rays emitted by Earth are absorbed and reemitted by a cloud, with some rays going to the surface and some going upward toward space [N2-R3]. In other words, clouds act as partial barriers to surface emission while redistributing the radiation. This is why clouds reduce the radiation emission to space and thus result in a heating of the planet [N3-F3].

Clouds block outgoing longwave radiation from the surface by absorbing part of that radiation before it can escape to space [N3-R1]. The Earth energy budget source explains that the energy imbalance is determined by the balance between absorbed solar radiation and outgoing longwave radiation [N3-R2]. So, when clouds absorb surface longwave radiation, they reduce the amount that can escape directly to space, which changes the energy balance [N3-R1][N3-R2].

Cloud optical thickness and altitude change the effect because thicker clouds are more opaque and absorb more radiation, while higher clouds are colder and emit less longwave radiation [N2-R3][N3-F3]. The evidence also shows that cloud properties strongly affect the planetary albedo and OLR [N3-F3]. Although the provided evidence does not give a precise numerical altitude-dependent formula, it supports the general principle that cloud characteristics determine how much radiation is absorbed versus re-emitted [N2-R3][N3-F3].

### 3) Quantitative role in Earth’s energy budget and radiative forcing

Outgoing longwave radiation is a central part of Earth’s energy budget because it is the only way Earth loses energy to space and thus the only way the planet cools itself [N2-F2]. The Earth energy budget source states that the energy entering, reflected, absorbed, and emitted by the Earth system are the components of the Earth’s radiation budget, and that all outgoing energy is radiated into space in the form of longwave radiation [N3-R2]. In this context, OLR is not an isolated process but a core part of the planet’s energy balance, determining whether Earth is warming or cooling [N2-F2][N3-R2][N3-F3].

The numerical magnitude of cloud reduction in OLR is about 30 W·m⁻² on average [N2-R5]. This means clouds reduce Earth’s OLR by roughly 30 watts per square meter, which is a substantial contribution to Earth’s energy budget. The evidence also indicates that cloud effects are highly variable and difficult to predict because cloud properties and their changes remain challenging to forecast [N2-R5]. In the Earth radiation budget context, clouds are described as reducing the radiation emission to space and thus heating the planet, showing that cloud radiative effects are not simply a passive shield but an active component of energy redistribution [N3-F3].

Radiative forcing connects absorption/emission to warming by quantifying how much energy is retained in the climate system. The Earth energy budget source explains that the rate of change in Earth’s energy is governed by the balance between absorbed solar radiation (ASR) and outgoing longwave radiation (OLR), so the energy imbalance is ASR minus OLR [N3-R2]. The greenhouse effect source adds that when energy arrives at a higher rate than it leaves, the amount of energy in the climate system increases, temperatures tend to rise, and OLR increases as a result [N1-F1]. So radiative forcing is the net energy imbalance caused by changes in absorption/emission: if clouds or greenhouse gases reduce OLR, they increase the energy retained in the system, which can lead to warming [N1-F1][N3-R2].

### 4) How this creates the greenhouse effect

The greenhouse effect traps heat and raises surface temperatures because greenhouse gases in the atmosphere absorb most of the longwave radiation emitted by the Earth, reducing the rate at which the planet can cool off [N1-R1][N1-F1]. In practical terms, the Earth’s surface emits longwave radiation that is mostly absorbed by greenhouse gases, which then re-emit it back toward the surface and out to space [N1-F1][N2-F2]. This absorption and re-emission mean the planet retains more heat, which raises surface temperatures.

Atmospheric and cloud contributions combine to reduce net outgoing radiation by acting as partial barriers to cooling. The atmosphere absorbs and emits longwave radiation mainly through greenhouse gases, while nitrogen, oxygen, and argon do not [N1-F1][N2-F2]. Clouds further reduce outgoing longwave radiation by absorbing part of the surface’s longwave emission and re-emitting it, with some rays going downward toward the surface and some upward toward space [N2-R3]. The evidence also says clouds reduce the radiation emission to space and thus result in a heating of the planet [N3-F3]. In addition, the Earth energy budget source states that all outgoing energy is radiated into space in the form of longwave radiation, and that the energy imbalance is determined by the balance between absorbed solar radiation and outgoing longwave radiation [N3-R2]. So the combined effect is not just one-way absorption; the atmosphere and clouds both absorb and re-emit radiation, which means they reduce the net amount of energy escaping directly to space [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-R2].

This process is different from a simple one-way heat trap because the atmosphere and clouds do not merely block outgoing radiation permanently; instead, they absorb radiation and then re-emit it in all directions, including back toward the surface and out to space [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The greenhouse effect is therefore a radiative feedback mechanism that redistributes energy rather than storing it indefinitely. The Earth energy budget discussion emphasizes that the planet adjusts its temperature to keep the energy imbalance small, and that when energy arrives at a higher rate than it leaves, temperatures tend to increase [N3-R2]. In this context, the greenhouse effect and clouds together increase the amount of energy retained in the climate system, which can raise surface temperatures [N1-F1][N3-R2].

## Conclusion

In summary: the atmosphere and clouds reduce Earth’s outgoing longwave radiation by absorbing and re-emitting longwave radiation. Greenhouse gases like water vapor and carbon dioxide absorb most of the longwave radiation emitted by the Earth, while clouds absorb part of that radiation and re-emit it in multiple directions [N1-R1][N1-F1][N2-R3]. This reduces the amount of energy escaping directly to space, which means less cooling occurs and more heat is retained in the climate system [N2-F2][N3-F3]. The greenhouse effect is created when this retained heat raises surface temperatures, because the planet’s temperature adjusts to balance the energy entering and leaving the system [N1-F1][N3-R2]. The process is not a simple one-way heat trap, because the atmosphere and clouds redistribute radiation in all directions, changing the net energy balance rather than simply preventing cooling [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-R2].

In other words, clouds act as partial barriers to surface emission while redistributing the radiation. This is why clouds reduce the radiation emission to space and thus result in a heating of the planet [N3-F3].

Clouds block outgoing longwave radiation from the surface by absorbing part of that radiation before it can escape to space [N3-R1]. The Earth energy budget source explains that the energy imbalance is determined by the balance between absorbed solar radiation and outgoing longwave radiation [N3-R2]. So, when clouds absorb surface longwave radiation, they reduce the amount that can escape directly to space, which changes the energy balance [N3-R1][N3-R2].

Cloud optical thickness and altitude change the effect because thicker clouds are more opaque and absorb more radiation, while higher clouds are colder and emit less longwave radiation [N2-R3][N3-F3]. The evidence also shows that cloud properties strongly affect the planetary albedo and OLR [N3-F3]. Although the provided evidence does not give a precise numerical altitude-dependent formula, it supports the general principle that cloud characteristics determine how much radiation is absorbed versus re-emitted [N2-R3][N3-F3].

### 3) Quantitative role in Earth’s energy budget and radiative forcing

Outgoing longwave radiation is a central part of Earth’s energy budget because it is the only way Earth loses energy to space and thus the only way the planet cools itself [N2-F2]. The Earth energy budget source states that the energy entering, reflected, absorbed, and emitted by the Earth system are the components of the Earth’s radiation budget, and that all outgoing energy is radiated into space in the form of longwave radiation [N3-R2]. In this context, OLR is not an isolated process but a core part of the planet’s energy balance, determining whether Earth is warming or cooling [N2-F2][N3-R2][N3-F3].

The numerical magnitude of cloud reduction in OLR is about 30 W·m⁻² on average [N2-R5]. This means clouds reduce Earth’s OLR by roughly 30 watts per square meter, which is a substantial contribution to Earth’s energy budget. The evidence also indicates that cloud effects are highly variable and difficult to predict because cloud properties and their changes remain challenging to forecast [N2-R5]. In the Earth radiation budget context, clouds are described as reducing the radiation emission to space and thus heating the planet, showing that cloud radiative effects are not simply a passive shield but an active component of energy redistribution [N3-F3].

Radiative forcing connects absorption/emission to warming by quantifying how much energy is retained in the climate system. The Earth energy budget source explains that the rate of change in Earth’s energy is governed by the balance between absorbed solar radiation (ASR) and outgoing longwave radiation (OLR), so the energy imbalance is ASR minus OLR [N3-R2]. The greenhouse effect source adds that when energy arrives at a higher rate than it leaves, the amount of energy in the climate system increases, temperatures tend to rise, and OLR increases as a result [N1-F1]. So radiative forcing is the net energy imbalance caused by changes in absorption/emission: if clouds or greenhouse gases reduce OLR, they increase the energy retained in the system, which can lead to warming [N1-F1][N3-R2].

### 4) How this creates the greenhouse effect

The greenhouse effect traps heat and raises surface temperatures because greenhouse gases in the atmosphere absorb most of the longwave radiation emitted by the Earth, reducing the rate at which the planet can cool off [N1-R1][N1-F1]. In practical terms, the Earth’s surface emits longwave radiation that is mostly absorbed by greenhouse gases, which then re-emit it back toward the surface and out to space [N1-F1][N2-F2]. This absorption and re-emission mean the planet retains more heat, which raises surface temperatures.

Atmospheric and cloud contributions combine to reduce net outgoing radiation by acting as partial barriers to cooling. The atmosphere absorbs and emits longwave radiation mainly through greenhouse gases, while nitrogen, oxygen, and argon do not [N1-F1][N2-F2]. Clouds further reduce outgoing longwave radiation by absorbing part of the surface’s longwave emission and re-emitting it, with some rays going downward toward the surface and some upward toward space [N2-R3]. The evidence also says clouds reduce the radiation emission to space and thus result in a heating of the planet [N3-F3]. In addition, the Earth energy budget source states that all outgoing energy is radiated into space in the form of longwave radiation, and that the energy imbalance is determined by the balance between absorbed solar radiation and outgoing longwave radiation [N3-R2]. So the combined effect is not just one-way absorption; the atmosphere and clouds both absorb and re-emit radiation, which means they reduce the net amount of energy escaping directly to space [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-R2].

This process is different from a simple one-way heat trap because the atmosphere and clouds do not merely block outgoing radiation permanently; instead, they absorb radiation and then re-emit it in all directions, including back toward the surface and out to space [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The greenhouse effect is therefore a radiative feedback mechanism that redistributes energy rather than storing it indefinitely. The Earth energy budget discussion emphasizes that the planet adjusts its temperature to keep the energy imbalance small, and that when energy arrives at a higher rate than it leaves, temperatures tend to increase [N3-R2]. In this context, the greenhouse effect and clouds together increase the amount of energy retained in the climate system, which can raise surface temperatures [N1-F1][N3-R2].

## Conclusion

In summary: the atmosphere and clouds reduce Earth’s outgoing longwave radiation by absorbing and re-emitting longwave radiation. Greenhouse gases like water vapor and carbon dioxide absorb most of the longwave radiation emitted by the Earth, while clouds absorb part of that radiation and re-emit it in multiple directions [N1-R1][N1-F1][N2-R3]. This reduces the amount of energy escaping directly to space, which means less cooling occurs and more heat is retained in the climate system [N2-F2][N3-F3]. The greenhouse effect is created when this retained heat raises surface temperatures, because the planet’s temperature adjusts to balance the energy entering and leaving the system [N1-F1][N3-R2]. The process is not a simple one-way heat trap, because the atmosphere and clouds redistribute radiation in all directions, changing the net energy balance rather than simply preventing cooling [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-R2].
